mcqs.question: In little-endian memory layout, which byte of a multi-byte value is stored at the lowest memory address?
options: The most-significant byte
It's random and determined at runtime
Always the zero byte
The least-significant byte
mcqs.explanation: Little-endian stores the least-significant byte first (at the lowest address) -- the mnemonic is 'little end first'. Big-endian does the opposite, storing the most-significant byte first.

mcqs.question: Why do little-endian machines need functions like htonl/ntohl before sending multi-byte values over the network?
options: Because network protocols standardized on big-endian byte order, so little-endian hosts must swap bytes to match the wire format
Because TCP/IP only transmits single-byte values
Because the network card doesn't support little-endian data
htonl/ntohl are only needed for floating-point numbers, not integers
mcqs.explanation: Network byte order is big-endian by long-standing convention. Little-endian machines (most modern hardware) must byte-swap multi-byte fields via htonl/ntohl to match that convention when sending or receiving over the network.

mcqs.question: What typically happens when you parse a binary file or packet using the wrong endianness assumption?
options: The program immediately crashes with a clear error message
It silently produces a different, plausible-looking but incorrect numeric value -- no error is raised
The operating system automatically detects and corrects the mistake
Only floating-point fields are affected, integers are unaffected
mcqs.explanation: Reading bytes with the wrong endianness assumption doesn't fail loudly -- it just reinterprets the same bytes as a different, still-valid-looking number, which is exactly what makes this bug class dangerous (e.g., a corrupted length field driving a bad buffer size).

mcqs.question: A big-endian wire value of 42 gets read as little-endian without conversion, becoming a huge number. What does this illustrate about endianness bugs?
options: They don't crash or error at the point of the mistake -- they silently produce a different, entirely plausible-looking wrong value that causes problems downstream
The read operation itself fails immediately with an explicit endianness error
The value becomes negative, which is always easy to detect and guard against
This only happens with values larger than 16 bits
mcqs.explanation: Reading bytes in the wrong order produces a different but still valid-looking 32-bit number -- there's no error at the read itself. The bug surfaces later, wherever that value gets used (an allocation size, a loop bound), which is exactly why explicit byte-swap calls at wire boundaries matter: the mistake is invisible until something downstream misbehaves.

mcqs.question: Why is hand-rolling a C struct with bitfields to match a wire protocol's bit-field diagram considered risky?
options: Bit packing within a byte via compiler bitfields is compiler- and platform-dependent, separate from and not fixed by handling byte order correctly
C bitfields automatically handle both byte and bit order correctly on every platform
Bitfields are slower than byte order conversion functions like ntohl/htonl
Wire protocols never specify bit order, only byte order, so this concern doesn't apply
mcqs.explanation: Byte order (endianness) and bit order within a byte are separate concerns. C compiler bitfield layout is notoriously non-portable across compilers and platforms, so even correct byte-order handling doesn't guarantee the bits within each byte pack the way a protocol diagram assumes -- which is why production code favors explicit shift-and-mask operations over compiler bitfields for wire formats.
